content:
The late Princess Diana's youngest brother, Charles Spencer, has alleged in a new book that the heir apparent, Charles, once said Princess Diana would be quickly forgotten after her untimely passing in 1997, according to excerpts from an upcoming memoir.

According to excerpts from the new book "A Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," published by the Daily Mail on Wednesday, Spencer claimed he and the current British monarch had a heated phone argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in their mother's funeral procession.

In the book, due out next week, Spencer wrote: "Prince Charles continued with a tirade, and I didn't interrupt him. Then he paused for a moment."

He wrote: "I thought that pause was him trying to control himself, but then he burst out on the phone with what I have always believed was his contempt for Diana, and his fear that the whole world had gone mad over her death. 'Don't worry,' he said through gritted teeth, 'she'll be forgotten soon enough!'"

Spencer wrote that he was "stunned into silence" by the remarks and took several seconds to respond.

He wrote: "I said coldly, 'I really cannot believe you said that.' Then I hung up immediately."

The Daily Mail reported on Tuesday that four copies of Spencer's book had been stolen from a van in the Netherlands, with Dutch authorities investigating the burglary.

A publishing industry insider described the theft as "highly suspicious," telling the media: "This kind of thing has never happened before."

The source told the Daily Mail: "This is probably the most high-profile book of the year, and security has always been extremely tight."

Spencer's representatives did not immediately respond to HuffPost's inquiries.

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson, in a statement responding to HuffPost, said: "While we would not comment on books as a matter of course, His Majesty understands the pain siblings can cause to judgment, reason, and memory, even after many years—effects that are difficult for outsiders to perceive."

Spencer delivered a moving eulogy at Diana's funeral held at Westminster Abbey, mentioning the relentless intrusion of British tabloids and describing Diana as "the most pursued person in modern society."

In a recent social media post, Spencer said the upcoming book is "the most personal of the ten books I've written in the past thirty years."

He wrote: "At its core, this book is a younger brother's simplest tribute to an extraordinary sister."

Callie Lehnert contributed to this report.
